theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: What is the first step in planning a work activity?
options: Start cutting the steel so that time is not wasted
Order extra materials in case something goes wrong
Read the work order and drawing to understand the job
Book the welding booth for the whole week

On the gate of the customer's house
In the welding machine's manual

questions.stem: Which of these is the best source of information about the safe use of a new grinder?

A friend who used one once

So that fewer people need to know what is going on with it

questions.stem: For a small welded frame, which order of work is correct?

A list of jobs that have been cancelled

options: So that you can leave the workshop early if you happen to finish fast
So that the customer pays by the minute

So that you never need to take a break

questions.stem: What does a bar chart (Gantt chart) show in a work plan?
options: When each task starts and finishes
How much each worker is paid
The welding current for each joint
The colours of paint to be used

questions.stem: The gate frame must be welded before the hinges can be fitted. In planning, what is this link between two tasks called?
options: A tolerance
A hold point
A dependency
A cut list

questions.stem: What is a "hazard"?
options: The chance that an accident will happen
A report written after an accident
A safety sign on the workshop wall
Anything that could cause harm

questions.stem: What is a "risk"?

questions.stem: When should the risk assessment for a task be done?

options: One strong person to lift it alone
Lifting it fast so that it is over quickly
Enough people or lifting equipment, and a safe method
Waiting until the end of the day when everyone else has gone home

The type, size, grade and quantity needed
How heavy the steel is to lift alone
Which colour the customer likes

questions.stem: Why should the work plan be checked with the supervisor before starting?

Because supervisors enjoy reading long documents in their spare time

questions.stem: What is a short meeting at the start of a job, to tell the team the plan and the hazards, often called?

A job interview
A sales meeting

questions.stem: Which is the best plan for steel offcuts from a job?

questions.stem: When is a work activity complete?

questions.stem: What is the purpose of reviewing a job after it is finished?

To change the drawing to match what was made

questions.stem: When setting a target for a task, what do the letters SMART stand for?

Safe, Main, Active, Ready, Tested
Strong, Measured, Assembled, Riveted, Tacked

questions.stem: You have three jobs due. Which should usually be planned first?
options: The one you enjoy doing the most
The most urgent and important one

questions.stem: The drawing does not show the weld size for one joint. What should you do?
options: Use the biggest weld you can, to be safe
Leave that joint unwelded

questions.stem: Which of these is a hazard you should list when planning a grinding and welding job?
options: The colour of the workshop walls
The number of windows in the office
The make and model of the computer in the store room
Flying sparks, hot metal, noise and fumes

questions.stem: Why should the plan list the PPE needed for each task?
options: So that the right PPE is ready and in good condition
So that the PPE can be lent out to visitors to the workshop
So that only the supervisor wears PPE
So that PPE is worn only when the assessor looks

questions.stem: Before starting, how should the work area be prepared?
options: Leave it just as the last group left it
Pile all the materials in the walkway, ready to use
Clear, safe and set out with the tools and materials needed
Covered in sawdust to soak up oil

questions.stem: Why is it useful to estimate the cost of materials when planning?
options: To check the job can be done within budget
To decide which worker is the best welder
To find out the weather for the week
To know how many tea breaks the whole team can take

questions.stem: During the job, the customer asks to change the height of the gate. What should happen?
options: Make the change quietly and say nothing to anyone
Refuse straight away and tell the customer it is far too late
Make the gate both heights to keep everyone happy
Record the change, get it approved and update the plan

questions.stem: A job is falling behind the plan. Which is the best action?
options: Skip the quality checks to catch up
Tell the supervisor and agree a way to catch up safely
Work right through all the breaks without telling anyone at all
Stop wearing PPE so you can work faster

questions.stem: What is a method statement?
options: A bank statement for the cost of the job
A step-by-step plan of how a job will be done safely
A list of names of everyone in the workshop
A note from the customer saying they are happy with the job

questions.stem: Which plan helps to save materials?
options: Cut every piece from a new length of steel
Cut the shortest pieces first from each length
Cut the pieces in any order at all, as it makes no difference to waste

questions.stem: At the end of a job, what should be reported to the supervisor?
options: Work done, problems found, materials used and any faults
Only the time you went home
Nothing, as the finished work speaks for itself

questions.stem: After the job, what should be done with the tools and equipment?
options: Leave them on the bench for the next group
Take them home to keep them safe

essays.stem: Describe the steps you would follow to plan a complete work activity, such as making a steel gate, from receiving the job to handing it over.
essays.modelAnswer: First I read the work order and drawing carefully so that I understand what the customer wants: the size, material, finish and the date it is due. If anything is unclear, I ask the supervisor. Next I break the job into steps in a sensible order, for example measure, mark out, cut, clean, fit and tack, weld, grind, fit hinges and lock, paint and deliver. I make a cut list and a materials list, check what is in stock and order what is missing. I list the tools, machines and PPE needed and check that they are available and working. I estimate the time for each step and make a simple bar chart. I carry out a risk assessment and plan the controls, such as screens, extraction and a fire extinguisher. I add quality checks at key stages. I agree the plan with the supervisor and brief the team. During the job I check progress and quality, and at the end I clean up, hand over the gate, report and review the job.
markingPoints: Reads the work order and drawing and clarifies anything unclear
Breaks the job into steps in a sensible order
Plans materials (cut list), tools, equipment and PPE
Estimates time, carries out a risk assessment and adds quality checks
Agrees the plan, briefs the team, monitors progress, then cleans up, reports and reviews

essays.stem: Explain how you would find out and confirm exactly what a job requires before you start planning it.
essays.modelAnswer: I start with the work order or job card, which says what is to be made, how many, for whom and by when. I then study the drawing for the sizes, tolerances, material, joint types and weld sizes, and check that it is the latest revision. I read any specification or welding procedure for the job, which tells me the grade of steel, the process, the consumables and the finish. If the job is to fit something on site, such as burglar bars for a window, the opening must be measured, or I check that the measurements on the drawing were taken on site. I look at the maker's instructions for any special equipment and the safety data sheets for paints or chemicals. Where information is missing or two documents do not agree, I write down my questions and ask the supervisor or the customer. I record the answers on the job card, so that everyone works from the same information, before the plan is written.
markingPoints: Reads the work order or job card (what, how many, for whom, when)
Studies the drawing and checks its revision
Reads the specification, procedure, maker's instructions or safety data sheets
Checks or takes site measurements where the job must fit
Asks the supervisor or customer about anything missing or unclear, and records the answers

essays.stem: Explain how to work out the materials needed for a job, including making a cut list, and how to keep waste low.
essays.modelAnswer: First I study the drawing and list every part, with its material, section size, length and the number needed. This is the cut list. For example, a frame 1200 mm by 800 mm in 40 mm square tube needs 2 pieces at 1200 mm and 2 pieces at 800 mm, depending on how the corners are joined. I add the lengths of each section size together and allow a little for each saw cut and for squaring the ends. Then I work out how many stock lengths to order; the steel is often sold in 6 m lengths, so I plan which pieces will come from each length so that the offcuts are as small as possible. I also list other materials, such as electrodes or wire, grinding discs, paint and fixings. I check what is already in stock, including useful offcuts, before ordering the rest. To keep waste low, I cut the longest pieces first, measure twice before cutting, and keep useful offcuts, marked with their size, for later jobs.
markingPoints: Lists every part from the drawing with material, size, length and quantity (the cut list)
Totals the lengths and allows for saw cuts and squaring
Works out the number of stock lengths and plans which pieces come from each
Lists other materials and checks stock and offcuts before ordering
Keeps waste low: cutting plan, measuring twice, keeping useful offcuts

essays.stem: Describe how to carry out a simple risk assessment for a welding and grinding task, using the hierarchy of controls.
essays.modelAnswer: First, list each step of the task, such as cutting, grinding, welding and moving the finished part. For each step, identify the hazards: arc light, fumes, sparks and fire, hot metal, electric shock, noise, flying particles from grinding, and heavy lifting. Then decide who could be harmed and how likely and how serious the harm could be; this is the risk. Next, choose controls, starting at the top of the hierarchy. First, try to eliminate the hazard, for example by buying steel already cut to size so there is less grinding. Then substitute something safer, such as a quieter tool. Then use engineering controls, such as welding screens, fume extraction and guards on grinders. Then use administrative controls, such as a hot work permit, training, signs and keeping others away. Last, use PPE such as a helmet, gloves, safety glasses and ear protection. Write the assessment down, explain it to the team, and check it again if the job changes.
markingPoints: Breaks the task into steps and identifies the hazards
Judges who could be harmed and how likely and serious it is (the risk)
Uses the hierarchy in order: eliminate, substitute, engineering, administrative, PPE
Gives sensible welding and grinding examples for the controls
Records it, explains it to the team and reviews it if the job changes

essays.stem: Explain how you would estimate the time for a job and set out a simple schedule, such as a bar chart.
essays.modelAnswer: First I list the tasks in the order they must be done, for example marking out, cutting, cleaning, fitting and tacking, welding, grinding, inspection and painting. For each task I estimate the time, using past jobs, the advice of experienced workers or the supervisor, and the number of people and machines available. I add time for setting up, for drying paint, and for checks at the hold points, and I allow a little extra in case something goes wrong. I note which tasks depend on others, such as welding before painting, and which can be done at the same time by different people. Then I draw a bar chart: the tasks are listed down the left side, the days or hours run along the top, and each task is shown as a bar from its start to its finish. The chart shows the finish date, so I can check it meets the deadline. During the job I mark progress on the chart and update it if things change.
markingPoints: Lists the tasks in order
Estimates each task from experience, advice and the people and machines available
Allows for set-up, checks, drying time and a little extra
Shows which tasks depend on others and which can run at the same time
Draws the bar chart correctly, checks the deadline and updates it during the job

essays.stem: Explain why a work plan must be agreed with the supervisor and shared with the team, and say what you would tell the team at the start of the job.
essays.modelAnswer: The supervisor must agree the plan because they can spot mistakes or missing steps, make sure it fits other work in the shop, approve the cost and materials, and arrange any permits. Sharing the plan with the team makes sure everyone knows the job, works in the same way and understands the hazards, so that nobody does the wrong task or puts others at risk. At the start of the job I would hold a short toolbox talk. I would explain what we are making and show the drawing, the order of the steps and who is doing each task. I would tell the team the deadline and the hold points where work must stop for checking. I would go through the main hazards and controls from the risk assessment, the PPE to wear, where the fire extinguisher and first-aid box are, and what to do in an emergency. Finally, I would ask if anyone has questions and make sure everyone knows who to report problems to.
markingPoints: Supervisor checks for mistakes, approves cost and materials and arranges permits
Sharing the plan means everyone knows the job and the hazards
Toolbox talk: the job, drawing, steps and who does what
Deadline, hold points, hazards, controls, PPE and emergency arrangements
Invites questions and says who to report problems to

essays.stem: Describe what you would do if something goes wrong with your plan during the job, such as late materials or a broken machine.
essays.modelAnswer: First, I would stop and make the situation safe. If a machine has broken down, I switch it off, isolate it, tag it out of use and report it, and I do not try to repair it unless I am trained and allowed to. Then I tell the supervisor straight away what has happened and how it affects the plan. Together we look at the contingency plan or think of other options. For late materials, we might do other tasks first that do not need them, such as preparing jigs or painting parts already made, or get the materials from another supplier. For a broken machine, we might use another machine in the shop or change the order of work. If the deadline cannot be met, the supervisor tells the customer early and agrees a new date. I then update the plan and the bar chart, tell the team about the changes, and write down what happened so that it can be discussed at the review and planned for next time.
markingPoints: Makes the situation safe; isolates and tags a faulty machine
Reports to the supervisor straight away
Uses the contingency plan or sensible options (other tasks first, other supplier or machine)
Customer told early if the deadline changes
Updates the plan, tells the team and records what happened

essays.stem: Describe how to plan the tools, equipment and work area for a job, and the checks you would make before starting.
essays.modelAnswer: From the list of steps, I write down each tool and machine needed, for example measuring and marking tools, a cut-off saw, an angle grinder, clamps, a welding machine and its consumables, and the PPE for each task. I check that they are free when needed and book shared machines, such as the bandsaw or a welding booth. Before starting, I check each item: power tools and leads for damage and current test tags, guards in place, grinding discs the right type and undamaged, welding cables and clamps in good order, and measuring tools in calibration. Faulty items are tagged and reported, not used. I plan the work area so that materials flow in a sensible order from the store to cutting, welding and finishing, with clear walkways, no trailing cables, screens around welding, and nothing that can burn nearby. I check that the fire extinguisher, first-aid box and fume extraction are in place and working. Finally, I check that everyone has the right PPE.
markingPoints: Lists the tools, machines, consumables and PPE for each step
Checks they are available and books shared equipment
Checks condition: leads, test tags, guards, discs, cables and calibration; tags faulty items
Plans a safe, sensible layout: clear walkways, screens, no combustibles
Checks the extinguisher, first aid, extraction and PPE before starting

essays.stem: Explain how you would check progress and quality during a job, and what records you would keep.
essays.modelAnswer: I compare the work done with the plan at set times, for example at the end of each session, and mark progress on the bar chart. If a task is taking longer than planned, I find out why and tell the supervisor early, so that we can agree what to do. I also check quality at each stage, not only at the end. After cutting, I check the lengths and angles against the cut list and drawing. After fitting and tacking, I check the sizes and squareness, and at the hold points I wait for the supervisor or inspector to check before welding. After welding, I check the weld sizes and look for faults, and I check that the parts have not distorted. I keep records on the job card or inspection sheet: the tasks done and when, the time taken, materials used, the results of each check, any faults and what was done about them, and my name and the date. These records show that the work was done properly and help with the review.
markingPoints: Compares progress with the plan at set times and marks the chart
Finds the reason for delays and tells the supervisor early
Checks quality at each stage (cut, fit-up, hold points, after welding)
Records tasks, time, materials, check results and faults
Records are signed and dated and used to show the work and for the review

essays.stem: Describe what should be done at the end of a work activity, including clean-up, reporting and review.
essays.modelAnswer: When the work is finished, it is given a final inspection against the drawing and specification, and the results are recorded. Then the work area is cleaned up. Machines are switched off and isolated, gas cylinders are closed, and tools are cleaned, checked and returned to the store; any damaged tools are reported. Useful offcuts are marked and put back on the rack, scrap metal goes in the scrap bin, and other waste such as empty tins and used discs is disposed of in the right bins. The floor is swept and walkways are cleared. Next, the job card, inspection records and a list of materials used and time taken are completed and handed to the supervisor, with a report of any problems, faults or near misses. The finished item is handed over to the customer or the store. Finally, the team reviews the job: what went well, what went wrong, how the actual time and materials compared with the plan, and what to do differently next time.
markingPoints: Final inspection against the drawing, with results recorded
Machines and gas made safe; tools cleaned, checked and returned; damage reported
Offcuts, scrap and other waste sorted and disposed of correctly; area swept
Job card, records, materials and time handed in, with problems reported
Review compares actual with plan and notes what to improve

practical1.title: Write a full work plan for a customer's fabrication job and present it
practical1.brief: The assessor plays the supervisor and gives the group a customer's request with a drawing: for example, Mrs Campbell of Spanish Town wants a mild steel burglar bar grill for a 900 mm × 1200 mm window, due in five working days. As a group, write a complete work plan on the Centre's planning sheets: the list of steps in order; a cut list and materials list with quantities, and a cost estimate in J$ using the price list given; the tools, machines and PPE needed; a risk assessment with controls; a time estimate and a bar chart drawn on chart paper; and the quality checks and hold points. Each member is responsible for at least one part of the plan, and every member checks one other member's part. Finally, the group presents the plan to the supervisor, with each member explaining their own part and answering questions. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: The customer's request and drawing, given by the assessor
A supplier price list in J$ for steel, consumables and paint
Blank planning sheets: steps, cut list, materials list, risk assessment, quality checks
Chart paper, ruler and markers for the bar chart
photos: The group reading the drawing and the customer's request
The completed steps list and cut list
The materials list and cost estimate
The bar chart on chart paper
The quality checks and hold points
Each member presenting their part of the plan to the supervisor
checklist: Read the drawing and request correctly and raised any questions with the supervisor
Completed their part of the plan clearly and correctly
Calculations for lengths, quantities, cost or time were correct
Hazards and controls were sensible and followed the hierarchy of controls
Checked another member's part and helped correct any errors
Explained their part of the plan clearly and answered questions
Worked well with the group and kept to the time allowed
safety: Keep the planning area clear of the workshop's machines and hot work
Wear safety boots and glasses if the group goes into the workshop to check materials or tools
Do not touch or test machines while checking that they are available
Include the correct PPE, fire precautions and fume control in the plan

practical2.title: Plan and make a small welded frame, then review the job against the plan
practical2.brief: As a group, plan and make a small rectangular frame, about 400 mm × 300 mm, in 25 mm mild steel angle, to the assessor's drawing. First, write a short plan: the steps in order, the cut list, who does each task, the time for each step, the hazards and controls, and the checks. The assessor approves the plan before work starts. Then carry out the job as planned, with every member doing at least one practical task (marking out, cutting, cleaning, tacking, welding, grinding or checking) while the assessor watches. Write the actual start and finish time of each step on the plan as you go. When the frame is finished and checked, clean up, then fill in a review sheet together comparing the actual time and materials with the plan, and writing down two things to do better next time. Photograph each stage below and add the photos to the group's practical.
materials: 25 mm × 25 mm × 3 mm mild steel angle, about 1.6 m
The frame drawing, a blank plan sheet and a review sheet
Steel rule, tape measure, try square, scriber or marker
Hacksaw or cut-off saw, angle grinder with flap disc, files and clamps
Welding machine and consumables as the Centre uses (MMAW or MIG)
Full PPE for cutting, grinding and welding
photos: The written plan, signed as approved by the assessor
Marking out with the cut list beside the steel
Cut pieces laid out and labelled
The frame tacked and checked for square
The finished, welded frame being measured
The plan sheet showing the actual times beside the planned times
The work area cleaned and tools returned
checklist: Helped write the plan, including steps, cut list, times and hazards
Did their planned task correctly and safely, wearing the right PPE
Followed the agreed order of work and stopped for checks
Finished frame within the drawing's sizes and square
Took part in clean-up and returned tools in good condition
Took part in the review and suggested a sensible improvement
safety: Wear safety glasses and a face shield when grinding; check the disc is right for the grinder and undamaged
Clamp work firmly before cutting or grinding
Weld only in a booth or behind screens; wear full welding PPE
Remove anything that can burn and keep a fire extinguisher at hand
Treat all metal as hot after cutting or welding: use tongs and mark hot work
